implementation_notes: An empty class's identity is its type, so tag types - std::true_type, std::false_type, std::integral_constant and the iterator category tags - mark compile-time facts and select overloads through overload resolution rather than a run-time test; the classic interface-with-no-methods structure is replaced by passing a tag to a dispatch function. The standard library uses the same empty tag classes (std::in_place_t, std::nullopt_t) to disambiguate constructors. Prefer tag dispatch when the branch bodies deserve names, when you want the ordered fallback chain that tag inheritance provides, or when the toolchain predates C++17.
pitfalls: An empty struct still occupies one byte as a member; pass tags as unnamed by-value parameters, not as stored data.
The tag hierarchy decides overload priority: exact match beats direct base beats base-of-base, so a wrong inheritance order silently changes the selected implementation.
Tag dispatch selects at compile time only - without RTTI or a discriminant there is nothing to test on a polymorphic object at run time.

variants.name: Empty polymorphic marker base class
variants.idiom_name: abstract base with a virtual destructor, recognised with dynamic_cast
variants.implementation_notes: The classic OO form is an abstract base class with a virtual destructor and no other members, so dynamic_cast<const Marker *>(p) tests the mark at run time across unrelated hierarchies. It costs a vptr on every subclass, needs RTTI enabled, and the mark is inherited by all descendants exactly as in Java. Keep it for genuine cross-hierarchy recognition where a run-time test is required; otherwise the compile-time tag expresses the same intent more cheaply.
pitfalls: dynamic_cast needs RTTI, which some embedded toolchains disable, and it is slower than a non-polymorphic type test.
The vptr makes every marked object larger, so a marker is not free as it is in Java's interface metadata.
dynamic_cast across shared-library boundaries can fail on some ABIs when the type information is not merged.

variants.name: C++20 concepts as named compile-time markers
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 concepts turn the marker into a named compile-time predicate usable directly in template constraints and overload resolution, deleting the tag type and the _impl helper; a marker typedef in the type is required structurally and then checked by the concept. Use concepts for new code where the mark is a compile-time capability and you want readable constraint errors; they cannot express a run-time fact, and structural matching means the tag member must be documented as the nominal marker.
pitfalls: Concepts are structural, not nominal: any type that happens to declare the tag member satisfies the constraint unless the tag type itself is required to match.
Constraint subsumption rules decide which overload wins, so overlapping concepts need care or an explicit requires clause.
Concepts exist only at compile time; a run-time test still needs RTTI, a discriminant or a type list.
